explanations.explanation: Luke says, “They were talking with each other about everything that had happened.” (Luke 24:14) Seven miles is a long stretch of road, and these two had plenty on their minds. If I walked that far with a friend, I'd run out of things to say by mile two and start humming.

The text says the opposite. They were talking with each other about everything that had happened (Luke 24:14). So this was no silent walk with two people staring at their sandals. Two friends, one long road and a whole lot to sort through.

explanations.answer: Their eyes are kept from recognizing Him
explanations.explanation: Luke says, “…their eyes were kept from recognizing Him.” (Luke 24:16) Jesus is right there beside them and they don't know it's Him. The text says their eyes were kept from it, and it doesn't tell us more than that. You know when someone waves at you at the gym and you have no idea who it is? Same problem, much bigger moment.

explanations.answer: He walks without saying a single word
explanations.explanation: He actually speaks up pretty quick. Jesus asks them, “What are you discussing so intently as you walk along?” (Luke 24:17) So He isn't a silent walking buddy. The strange part is that they don't recognize Him while He talks with them.

explanations.answer: He stays a few steps behind them
explanations.explanation: Luke says Jesus Himself came up and walked along with them (Luke 24:15). That puts Him right beside them, not trailing back. Nobody is lagging behind here. The strange part is who they don't realize is walking next to them.

Luke says, “They stood still, with sadness on their faces.” (Luke 24:17) They had just been talking about everything that happened to Jesus. I think a face that heavy says a lot before anybody opens their mouth. Those two weren't hiding a thing.

Joy doesn't show up on their faces here. Luke says they stood still, with sadness on their faces (Luke 24:17). They're about to explain how they saw things going, and it's a heavy story. Hold on to that sadness, because it's where this scene starts.

The text names a different feeling. They stood still, with sadness on their faces (Luke 24:17). Nothing in the verse says they were angry. These two looked weighed down, and the stranger asking about it got an honest answer.

explanations.answer: If He's the only visitor who hasn't heard the news
explanations.explanation: Cleopas asks, “Are You the only visitor to Jerusalem who does not know the things that have happened there in recent days?” (Luke 24:18) I think he's amazed that the stranger hasn't heard. I bet those days felt huge to the two of them.

explanations.answer: If He's come to see the empty tomb
explanations.explanation: The empty tomb does come up, but not in this question. Cleopas asks if the stranger is the only visitor to Jerusalem who doesn't know what happened there in recent days (Luke 24:18). The women at the tomb only come into it a few verses later (Luke 24:22-23). So his question is about the news in general.

explanations.answer: If He's heading back home to Galilee today
explanations.explanation: Nobody mentions Galilee in this conversation. Cleopas asks whether the stranger is the only visitor to Jerusalem who doesn't know the things that have happened there (Luke 24:18). The two are the ones with a destination, a village called Emmaus. Cleopas is asking about the news, not travel plans.

explanations.answer: A prophet powerful in speech and action
explanations.explanation: They say, “This man was a prophet, powerful in speech and action before God and all the people.” (Luke 24:19) Powerful in what He said and powerful in what He did. That's how these two sum up Jesus of Nazareth. It's a big description, and they say it with sad faces.

explanations.answer: A rabbi who only taught in Galilee
explanations.explanation: They don't mention Galilee at all. They call Jesus of Nazareth “…a prophet, powerful in speech and action before God and all the people.” (Luke 24:19) Their description is about how powerful He was in speech and action, not about where He taught.

explanations.answer: A healer who stayed away from crowds
explanations.explanation: That's not how they describe Him. Cleopas and his friend say Jesus was powerful in speech and action “…before God and all the people.” (Luke 24:19) They say nothing about Him staying away from crowds.

They say, “Our chief priests and rulers delivered Him up to the sentence of death, and they crucified Him.” (Luke 24:20) That's how they tell it to the stranger. It's a heavy part of the story. I think the sadness on their faces fits.

Nazareth only shows up in His name, Jesus of Nazareth. The two say, “Our chief priests and rulers delivered Him up to the sentence of death, and they crucified Him.” (Luke 24:20) The text doesn't point to the people of Nazareth. This part of the story is heavy, so the details matter.

Nobody brings up Jericho or tax collectors in this walk. The two say it was their chief priests and rulers who delivered Jesus up to the sentence of death, and they crucified Him (Luke 24:20). Keep your eyes on who the text names. It's a heavy moment, and the details matter.

They say, “But we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel.” (Luke 24:21) Redeem is the word Luke gives us. Notice they say hoping, and that tells you where their hearts were on that road. It's a sad little sentence.

Rebuild isn't their word. They say, “But we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel.” (Luke 24:21) Notice it's “…we were hoping…” and not hoping right now. I think that tells you their hope felt shaky by then.

Judge isn't their word. They say, “But we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel.” (Luke 24:21) Their hope is about redeeming Israel, not judging it. I think that “were” in “…we were hoping…” sounds like a hope with a shadow over it.

They say, “…it is the third day since these things took place.” (Luke 24:21) They're counting days out loud. I think when your heart is heavy, you notice every one that passes. These two were keeping track.
They really do say it. Cleopas and his friend tell the stranger, “…it is the third day since these things took place.” (Luke 24:21) The third day is part of what they lay out for Him.

The two say the women “…had seen a vision of angels, who said that Jesus was alive.” (Luke 24:23) The women didn't find His body, and the angels said He was alive. That's the news the two bring up. They share it right alongside their sadness.

explanations.answer: That His body had been moved
explanations.explanation: That's not what they report. The two say the women saw a vision of angels, “…who said that Jesus was alive.” (Luke 24:23) Nothing about moving a body comes up in their telling. The angels' message was that Jesus was alive.

explanations.answer: That He would return next Sabbath
explanations.explanation: No Sabbath shows up in their report. The women saw a vision of angels, “…who said that Jesus was alive.” (Luke 24:23) That's the message the two repeat to the stranger. No dates, just that Jesus was alive.

The text says otherwise. Some of their companions went to the tomb and found it just as the women had described. Then comes the line, “But Him they did not see.” (Luke 24:24) They found the tomb as described, but they did not see Jesus.

That's right. The companions found the tomb just as the women had described, and the two say, “But Him they did not see.” (Luke 24:24) So the tomb matched the women's story, but the companions did not see Jesus. These two are still carrying a lot of questions on that road.

Jesus asks, “Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” (Luke 24:26) Suffer is the first blank. He puts it as a question: was it not necessary? He's pointing them to what the Christ was to go through.

Jesus says the Christ was to suffer these things “…and then to enter His glory?” (Luke 24:26) Glory is the second blank. The suffering comes first and then the glory, in that order. That's a lot to take in on a seven mile walk.

Escape isn't the word Jesus uses. He asks, “Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” (Luke 24:26) The question says suffer, and that's the first blank. Nothing in His words talks about getting away from it.

Prevent isn't in His question. Jesus asks, “Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” (Luke 24:26) The word for the first blank is suffer. His question points the other way from stopping anything.

Temple doesn't show up in this verse. Jesus says the Christ was to suffer these things “…and then to enter His glory?” (Luke 24:26) Glory is the word that fills the second blank. It's a close call if you're skimming, but the verse is clear.

explanations.answer: With Moses and all the Prophets
explanations.explanation: Luke says, “And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself.” (Luke 24:27) Moses and all the Prophets are where Jesus begins. From there, He explains what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself. I'd pay a month of cookie money to have heard that walk.

The text names a different starting point. Jesus began “…with Moses and all the Prophets…” and then explained what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself (Luke 24:27). The Psalms aren't named in this verse. Moses and all the Prophets are where Luke says He began.

explanations.answer: With the words of John the Baptist
explanations.explanation: John the Baptist, who came baptizing in the wilderness (Mark 1:4), isn't named here. Luke says Jesus began “…with Moses and all the Prophets…” and went on to all the Scriptures (Luke 24:27). So the starting point is Moses and the Prophets. It's a long walk with a lot of Scripture packed into it.

They pleaded with Him, “Stay with us, for it is nearly evening and the day is almost over.” (Luke 24:29) Pleaded is about as close to beg as you get. They didn't just say a polite goodbye. I think they weren't ready for that walk to end.

They aren't warning Him. Luke says they pleaded with Him, “Stay with us, for it is nearly evening and the day is almost over.” (Luke 24:29) That's an invitation, and a pretty heartfelt one. Beg is the word that fits.

Forbid would mean they were telling Him no. These two do the opposite. They pleaded with Him, “Stay with us, for it is nearly evening and the day is almost over.” (Luke 24:29) That's a request to stay, and a heartfelt one.

It looked like He was going farther, but then Luke says, “So He went in to stay with them.” (Luke 24:29) They asked, and He stayed. He didn't keep walking past Emmaus. The door opened for what happens at the table next.
That's right. Verse 28 says He seemed to be going farther, but after they pleaded with Him, “So He went in to stay with them.” (Luke 24:29) He accepted the invitation. The walk ended at the table.

explanations.answer: Their eyes are opened and they know Him
explanations.explanation: Luke says, “Then their eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus…” (Luke 24:31) Remember how their eyes were kept from recognizing Him earlier? Now that's changed. It all happens at the table, as He breaks the bread and gives it to them.

explanations.answer: They ask Him where He's really from
explanations.explanation: They don't ask Him anything here. Luke says their eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus (Luke 24:31). They knew Him. Questions about where He's from aren't part of this moment.

explanations.answer: They thank Him and say goodnight
explanations.explanation: No goodnights at this table. Luke says their eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus, “…and He disappeared from their sight.” (Luke 24:31) The moment moves fast. They know Him, and then He's gone from their sight.

explanations.answer: Their hearts were burning within them
explanations.explanation: They ask each other, “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32) They say it after they recognize Him. Looking back, they could tell something was happening inside them all along. I think that's a good feeling to look back on.

explanations.answer: Their hearts were stirred with anger
explanations.explanation: Anger isn't what they say. They ask, “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32) Burning is the word they use. Nothing in that verse says they were angry.

explanations.answer: Their hearts were racing with fear
explanations.explanation: Fear isn't in their words. They say, “Were not our hearts burning within us as He spoke with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32) Burning is the word they use. It sounds more like a warm glow than a scare.

The text says otherwise. Luke says, “And they got up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem.” (Luke 24:33) That very hour means no waiting around. If it were me, I'd have a long talk with the snooze button first.
That's right. They “…got up that very hour and returned to Jerusalem.” (Luke 24:33) No sleeping on it and no waiting for morning. They had news to share and they went.

When the two get there, they find the Eleven and those with them gathered together and saying, “The Lord has indeed risen and has appeared to Simon!” (Luke 24:34) Simon is a man the text names here without saying more. The news was already going around the room before the two said a word. They came with their own story and walked into one.

The text says the news was already in the room. The Eleven and those with them were gathered together and saying, “The Lord has indeed risen and has appeared to Simon!” (Luke 24:34) Simon is a man the text names here without giving more. So the two arrived to find the news waiting for them.
